1140.bp: When you search for an image in a massive database—say, finding similar product photos among billions—the system converts images into compact codes called hashes that let it search quickly instead of comparing full pictures. The real-world need: making this search fast and reliable, even when someone tries to fool the system by subtly distorting an image.
1140.wh: The tension sits between two opposing forces. To find similar images well, the neural network that creates these codes needs to respond across a wide range of frequencies—think of it like a radio picking up many channels at once. But when you train the system to resist attacks (adversarial training), you're forcing it to ignore variation, which collapses all those channels into just a few low frequencies. The system becomes blind to fine details that actually matter for retrieval.
1140.ap: The paper identifies this trade-off through spectral analysis—essentially looking at which mathematical frequencies the model is using. Their solution, SAAH, picks and chooses which frequencies to keep: it preserves the ones that help distinguish between different images and discards only the frequencies that are vulnerable to attack. This is surgical, not scorched-earth.
1140.ww: By keeping the signal for what makes images different while trimming only the fragile bits, you stop the adversarial collapse. The model can still see the full spectrum of patterns that matter for searching, so it doesn't sacrifice accuracy to gain robustness. It's like adding armour to the weak joints instead of encasing the whole structure in concrete.
1140.po: Experiments show the method achieves both good retrieval accuracy and resistance to adversarial attacks simultaneously, where previous methods had to pick one or the other. This means search systems can be deployed in hostile settings without giving up speed or relevance.

1141.bp: Knowledge graphs—gigantic networks of facts like 'Einstein studied physics' or 'Paris is the capital of France'—grow constantly. When new relationships emerge (maybe a new scientific finding), a system needs to reason about them using only a handful of examples, since collecting thousands would take forever. The goal: make the system smarter about new facts without forgetting old ones.
1141.wh: There's a buried trap in preservation. Previous systems focused on not forgetting old knowledge, which made sense. But the paper points out that some old knowledge actively conflicts with new facts—either contradicting them directly or warping how entities are represented in the network's memory. For instance, if a relation used to mean 'A owns B' but now means 'A operates B', the old pattern poisons reasoning about the new one. Just keeping everything backfires.
1141.ap: CSKU (the framework name) surgically removes conflicting knowledge rather than preserving all of it. It works at two levels: structurally, it identifies when old connection patterns contradict new ones and gradually weakens those old patterns during learning. Semantically, it finds when old relations are pulling the meaning of an entity in the wrong direction and dampens their influence. Both happen dynamically as the system learns new facts.
1141.ww: By deleting the right things instead of keeping everything, entity meanings stay coherent. The system stops being pulled in two directions by contradictory patterns, so it can focus its limited learning capacity on the new relation. It's not amnesia—it's unlearning what actively hurts.
1141.po: On real-world knowledge graph datasets, the method outperforms systems that simply preserve old knowledge. The few-shot learner can adapt faster to new relations without that conflicting baggage dragging it down.

1142.bp: When you ask a system a question about a document—'What is the author's position on climate policy?'—it first retrieves candidate pages, then reads them to generate an answer. The bottleneck is the retrieval step: it often pulls in irrelevant or noisy documents, burying the answer in a pile of junk. The goal is to rank retrieved documents in a smarter order so the reader sees useful ones first.
1142.wh: Existing reranking methods learn from human judgments or outputs from large language models, but those proxies don't always align with what actually makes an answer better. A document might be marked as 'relevant' but still not help the downstream system generate a correct answer. The system optimizes for the proxy, not the real goal.
1142.ap: AD-Reranker flips the problem: instead of imitating human labels, it treats reranking as a task where an agent (the reranker) interacts with an environment (the downstream reader). It assigns rewards based on whether the final answer is correct, then learns which ranking strategies lead to correct answers. It uses a policy method called GRPO to update itself based on groups of rankings rather than individual examples.
1142.ww: By optimizing directly for answer correctness rather than document relevance, the reranker learns which documents actually help reasoning. A document might not be perfectly topical but could supply a crucial fact. The method finds those unexpected gems because it grades them by whether they lead to right answers.
1142.po: In practice, integrating AD-Reranker into existing systems improves answer accuracy by 1.9–5.0% while cutting the computational tokens the reader needs to process by 15–52%. Same answer quality, much faster.

1143.bp: Search engines and new AI-powered information systems collect your queries—what you're looking for—and your reading patterns. This data can leak personal information: medical searches reveal health conditions, financial searches reveal wealth or debt. As these systems become more powerful and integrated, the privacy stakes grow sharply. The goal: design a research roadmap to keep systems effective while truly protecting user privacy.
1143.wh: Current privacy solutions are piecemeal and incomplete. Some protect queries from the server, others protect the documents you read, but few address the entire pipeline. More subtly, generative systems (which summarize documents into answers) can inadvertently regurgitate private information from the documents they've seen. It's unclear which privacy guarantees matter most, and there's no agreement on how to measure whether privacy is actually protected.
1143.ap: This perspective paper doesn't propose a single solution but rather defines a research agenda. It identifies key gaps: How do we prevent the systems from revealing personal information while still providing useful answers? How do we protect privacy throughout the entire process, not just at endpoints? It grounds its recommendations in actual user surveys and interviews with experts from academia, industry, and regulation.
1143.ww: By mapping the problem space first—identifying which privacy threats matter most to users and where current solutions fall short—the field can prioritize. The paper's research pillars give researchers a shared vocabulary and clear targets, preventing wasted effort on low-impact problems.
1143.po: The outcome is a roadmap for future work: what specific problems should be solved first, which combinations of privacy guarantees are most valuable, and how to evaluate whether privacy is truly protected. This focuses the research community rather than suggesting it already has the answers.

1144.bp: Information systems don't exist in isolation—they compete. A search engine battles a large language model for user attention. A recommendation system competes with others for which products a user sees. Evaluation today assumes each system works alone, but real deployment means survival in a marketplace where users switch, platforms make routing decisions, and resources are limited. The question: how do we measure whether a system will actually win?
1144.wh: Standard benchmarks measure accuracy in a vacuum, assuming one system is tested in isolation. But they miss competitive dynamics: an inferior system that launches early might capture enough users to dominate a later, better alternative. Early adoption advantages, switching costs, and path dependency shape outcomes as much as pure quality. Accuracy-only metrics can't predict post-deployment success.
1144.ap: Marketplace Evaluation simulates repeated interactions between users, agents, and competing systems over time. It models how user preferences evolve, how they switch between systems, and how resource constraints limit what each system can offer. Metrics shift from traditional accuracy measures to longitudinal ones: market share, user retention, sustainable competitive advantage.
1144.ww: By simulating the actual deployment environment—where users learn, drift, and make choices based on experience, not just first-impression accuracy—predictions become grounded in reality. The framework reveals which innovations survive competitive pressure versus which are brittle successes that collapse when challenged.
1144.po: Researchers can now evaluate whether an improvement in a lab actually matters in deployment. The framework identifies which competitive advantages are structural (hard to overcome) versus which are fragile. It extends TREC evaluation to include marketplace-level metrics beyond accuracy.

1145.bp: Large language model–based systems that let you 'chat with your documents' (asking questions about PDFs, emails, internal files) are rapidly replacing traditional search. Instead of seeing a ranked list that you browse, you see a conversational assistant that synthesizes an answer in a few sentences. The question: what mental models do users build about these systems, and do those models match how the systems actually work?
1145.wh: Users come to these new systems with assumptions shaped by their experience with search engines and analysts. They assume the system has read everything thoroughly, remembers it perfectly, and can find anything if it exists. But modern systems operate through selective retrieval—they pull only a few documents and reason over those, which is fast but has gaps. When users' mental models are wrong, they make bad decisions about what to trust.
1145.ap: Through interviews and observations, the paper documents what users actually think: most assume the system reads exhaustively and has perfect memory, not selective retrieval. This leads to specific behavioral shifts: they reformulate queries less (trusting the system to understand), delegate sense-making to the AI instead of verifying, rarely check the documents that were actually used, and treat 'not found' as proof something doesn't exist.
1145.ww: These behaviors make sense given their (incorrect) mental models. If you think the system is thorough, you don't need to try alternate queries or verify sources—it would have found the answer if it existed. But in truth, the system might have missed relevant documents. Users' incorrect assumptions lead to systematically worse decision-making.
1145.po: The insight is that interface design matters enormously: showing users the retrieval-then-synthesis pipeline explicitly could shift them toward more skeptical, verification-oriented behavior. The system isn't broken; users' expectations are misaligned with its actual design.

1146.bp: Modern search systems stack layers: first retrieving a large set of candidates, then ranking down to fewer options, then feeding those to a reader to synthesize an answer. Each stage costs computation. As systems grow more complex, the question becomes: can we precompute parts of ranking offline instead of recalculating everything at query time? The goal is speed without sacrificing accuracy.
1146.wh: Current systems treat relevance as purely query-dependent: the system asks 'how well does this document match the query?' at search time. But this ignores something obvious: some documents are useful for many queries (they're authoritative, cover broad topics), while others are niche. The design bakes in a computational bottleneck: all query-dependent scoring must happen when the user types.
1146.ap: The paper reframes relevance as a Bayesian posterior inference: combine a query-dependent component (how well does the query match?) with a query-independent prior (how generally useful is this document?). The prior can be computed once and cached offline. At query time, you only need to fuse precomputed scores, not rerank from scratch. It draws on classical probabilistic retrieval theory and applies it to modern neural systems.
1146.ww: By separating query-dependent and query-independent components, you can compute the expensive parts in advance. The mathematical decomposition exposes where you can shift work: ranking can happen offline for the priors, leaving only lightweight fusion for live queries. This preserves accuracy because the prior captures real document authority.
1146.po: Experiments show a learned prior improves first-stage retrieval (up to Δ nDCG@10 ≈ 3 or 4 points) with minimal query-time cost—just score fusion. In deployed systems, this means faster responses for users without accuracy loss.

1147.bp: Dementia affects over 50 million people globally. Current retrieval-augmented generation systems—which synthesize answers by reading documents—assume users can write coherent queries, interpret answers reliably, and remember context. None of these are safe assumptions for someone with dementia or cognitive impairment. The goal: redesign information systems for people whose cognitive state is unstable and variable.
1147.wh: Existing RAG systems are built for cognitively stable users. But with dementia, queries are inconsistent (the same question phrased differently each time), feedback is unreliable (a user might not accurately remember which answer was helpful), and cognitive load matters enormously (complex multi-clause answers overwhelm comprehension). Additionally, caregivers are often gatekeepers—they need to verify and oversee what information the person receives. Current systems are designed for a single autonomous user.
1147.ap: The paper proposes functional requirements for cognitively adaptive RAG: temporal user modelling that tracks how cognitive ability changes over time, caregiver-in-the-loop retrieval that lets a family member verify answers, consent-aware evidence access that respects fluctuating capacity to authorize information sharing, and cognitive-load-aware presentation that adjusts answer complexity to comprehension level. These aren't optional features—they're foundational redesigns.
1147.ww: By modelling users as cognitively dynamic (not stable), the system can adapt moment-to-moment. A caregiver's presence adds a verification layer, protecting against both misunderstanding and manipulation. Adaptive presentation keeps cognitive load manageable. Temporal tracking lets the system learn individual patterns rather than assuming all people with dementia need identical support.
1147.po: The outcome is a set of design principles grounded in participatory research with 41 members of dementia and MCI communities. These shift RAG from a consumer-grade model toward a healthcare-grade model that's actually usable by cognitively diverse populations.

1148.bp: Regulators increasingly mandate that certain information be forgotten: removed from search results, scrubbed from generated answers. The right to be forgotten in GDPR, takedown notices, and redaction orders all require systems to erase facts. The problem: retrieval-augmented systems (which read documents to generate answers) can delete a document but still regenerate the same fact from other sources or even infer it. How do you audit whether forgetting actually happened?
1148.wh: Current compliance checks are surface-level. They verify that a document was deleted from the retrieval database, but they don't verify that the system still generates the same forbidden fact in answers. A system might genuinely exclude the removed document but reconstruct the fact from context clues or other sources. Document-level compliance is insufficient if answers still leak the forbidden information.
1148.ap: Forgetting-by-Design (FBD) is an audit mechanism that runs before-and-after tests. It probes the system in two modes: one where the fact is revoked, one where it's allowed. It checks two channels independently: retrieval (does the system still cite the removed document?) and generation (does the answer still contain the forbidden fact?). It measures both compliance (did forgetting succeed?) and utility (did we lose access to lawful information that should still be available?).
1148.ww: By separating channels and measuring independently, the audit catches failures that single metrics miss. A system might suppress citation while still leaking facts in prose, or over-correct and hide lawful information. The before-after structure with matched controls mimics medical trials, giving clearer causal evidence.
1148.po: Applying FBD to real RAG systems reveals systematic compliance gaps: retrieval can be suppressed while answers still leak. The audit report card guides which interventions matter most and where over-corrections harm legitimate access.

1149.bp: Researchers measure information retrieval progress through metrics: does a new ranking method score higher on standard benchmarks than the old one? We interpret metric improvements as real progress—better systems. But metrics are abstractions: they measure small, simplified tasks, not the messy reality of what users actually need from search. The question: how do we know if our metrics are measuring what matters?
1149.wh: The validity gap is fundamental. A metric might improve because the system now ranks the most relevant document first, or because it learned to game the metric in ways users don't care about. As systems grow more powerful (especially with large language models as judges), the risk grows: optimizing toward an LLM's notion of relevance might not correlate with user satisfaction. We've abstracted so far from reality that improvements in metrics might mean nothing.
1149.ap: The paper proposes practical ways to discuss and improve evaluation validity. It asks: does the evaluation task resemble real information seeking? Are the measures aligned with what users actually want? Can we validate that metric improvements correspond to real improvements? These questions encourage researchers to design evaluations that reflect actual needs, not just convenience.
1149.ww: By connecting evaluation design explicitly to real-world outcomes, research stays grounded. If metrics improve but users don't prefer the result, the research was misdirected. Validity forces a reality check: are we optimizing the right thing?
1149.po: The outcome is methodological: researchers can make better choices about evaluation protocols, catch cases where metrics mislead, and optimize toward systems people actually want rather than systems that maximize numbers.

1150.bp: When researchers want to know whether a new ranking method beats an old one, they run a statistical test to see if the difference is 'significant' or just luck. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test is widely recommended as safer than the t-test for this task. It's the default choice in IR research for decades. But the paper argues this recommendation is dangerously wrong.
1150.wh: Wilcoxon was designed for small samples of paired measurements and assumes the data follows a specific structure. But IR benchmarks violate these assumptions dramatically. Metrics across topics are highly non-normal, correlated in complex ways, and collected from small pools of documents per topic. The test has a hidden failure mode: it loses control of false positives in exactly these conditions. Researchers might declare a system 'significantly better' when there's no real difference—and not notice because statistics textbooks don't fully explain the assumptions.
1150.ap: The paper reviews IR evaluation practices systematically, showing where Wilcoxon breaks down mathematically. It demonstrates through TREC data that the test frequently produces wrong conclusions. The fix isn't to pick a different test mechanically—it's to understand the actual structure of IR data and choose methods accordingly. For IR specifically, alternatives exist that don't assume normality but also don't break under realistic conditions.
1150.ww: By understanding the assumption violations, researchers can see why Wilcoxon fails. It's not a safe default; it's a trap. The cumulative effect across published papers is a field claiming statistical significance for improvements that don't reliably exist.
1150.po: The practical outcome: abandoning Wilcoxon in IR research improves methodological soundness. Researchers can choose tests that are actually appropriate for non-normal, correlated IR metrics and avoid false-positive discoveries that undermine field progress.

1151.bp: Information systems today are fragmented: search engines handle 'find me documents', recommenders handle 'suggest products I'd like', chatbots handle 'have a conversation'. Users constantly switch between them. The vision here is a unified system that can mix all three modes—search, recommendation, conversation—to help a person complete a task, whatever form that task takes. The goal: one system that adapts its interaction mode to what the person actually needs.
1151.wh: Separate systems miss the context that makes each mode effective. A person searching for a hotel might benefit from recommendations based on past bookings. A person browsing products might need a conversational explanation. Current systems don't share understanding of what the person is trying to do, so each starts from scratch. They also don't share user context, making interactions feel fragmented.
1151.ap: GIANT (General Intelligent Information Agent) is proposed as a unified framework. It models four things: the situation (what's happening right now), the content (what information is available), the task (what is the person trying to accomplish), and the user (their preferences and history). Using these models, the system decides whether to search, recommend, or converse—and what to show—to minimize the person's effort while staying resource-efficient. The core architecture uses a Markov Decision Process, which can optimize long-term outcomes rather than immediate answers.
1151.ww: By unifying the models, the system can learn when each mode helps most. A recommendation might be better than a search result if you're browsing. Conversation might save time if the person needs explanation. The MDP architecture plans ahead: this interaction might set up a better next move. Context flows between modes instead of each starting blind.
1151.po: The outcome is an architectural vision: how to formalize a unified agent and how to evaluate it using simulated users who behave realistically. This gives researchers a common framework instead of isolated optimization of search, recommendation, and conversation separately.

1152.bp: E-commerce platforms often bundle products: 'buy these three items together for a discount'. Bundle recommendations combine two steps: building good bundles from the catalog, then recommending which bundles to each customer. The question: do these steps actually work well together in practice, or is the whole pipeline weaker than the parts suggest?
1152.wh: Research has tackled bundle creation and bundle recommendation separately, with each showing progress. But in deployment, they're entangled: the bundles you offer shape what users see, and user feedback shapes which bundles you build. There's no comprehensive evaluation of the full pipeline, so it's unclear whether integration problems are hiding. Do item-level adjustments (swapping one product for another in a bundle) break recommendation models? Does cold-start (few user interactions) hit one stage harder?
1152.ap: The paper implements eight bundle-editing methods (ways to create bundles), nine item-level methods (ways to tweak bundles), and seven recommendation models across six real datasets. It runs them through a complete pipeline: edit → recommend → measure. This reproducibility study doesn't propose new methods but rather documents what works and what fails.
1152.ww: By measuring the full pipeline end-to-end, the paper exposes bottlenecks that single-stage research misses. A method might work well in isolation but break when integrated. The systematic evaluation across datasets and interaction densities reveals which failures are universal problems versus dataset-specific quirks.
1152.po: Key findings: bundle-level editing struggles to create high-quality bundles; item-level replacement is a universal bottleneck; recommendation models degrade when combined with editing; cold-start (sparse feedback) exacerbates all problems. This roadmap guides where future work should focus.

1153.bp: Modern retrieval-augmented generation systems use large language models to rephrase queries ('tennis player' becomes 'famous athlete in racket sports'). Different phrasings can retrieve different documents. Running the entire pipeline for every reformulation is expensive, so the question becomes: can you predict which variant will produce the best final answer before you incur the cost of retrieval and generation?
1153.wh: Traditional query performance prediction (QPP) estimates how 'hard' a query is—does it have clear answers? But here the problem is different: picking the best variant among many reformulations of the same question. Worse, the variants that maximize retrieval metrics (nDCG—getting relevant documents ranked high) often don't produce the best generated answers. There's a systematic divergence: what makes documents rank well doesn't always make answers good.
1153.ap: The paper evaluates pre- and post-retrieval prediction methods on variant selection across TREC-RAG benchmarks. Pre-retrieval predictors estimate variant quality before retrieving documents; post-retrieval ones estimate after seeing retrieval results. The key insight is measuring 'utility gap': how often do high-ranking variants (good for document ranking) fail to produce good answers?
1153.ww: By measuring the gap between retrieval and generation objectives, the work explains why simple ranking-based heuristics fail. A variant that retrieves authoritative-looking documents might still produce a worse answer if those documents don't align with the reasoning path the language model needs. The divergence is structural, not random.
1153.po: Practically, lightweight pre-retrieval predictors can often match or beat expensive post-retrieval methods at identifying variants that improve end-to-end quality. This enables fast filtering: discard clearly bad variants without full pipeline execution, run full pipeline only on promising candidates.

1154.bp: Large language models now rewrite queries to find better documents: 'tennis' becomes 'professional athletic competition in racket sports'. Many papers report query reformulation works great. But they test under different conditions: different LLMs, different datasets, different retriever types. The question: which results actually replicate, and which depend on one specific setup?
1154.wh: A method might work brilliantly with dense neural retrievers but fail with sparse keyword search. Larger language models don't always produce better reformulations. Results depend on implementation details: which prompts were used, which LLM, which retriever. Published papers don't standardize these choices, so you can't tell if an improvement is real or an artifact of favorable conditions.
1154.ap: The paper implements ten representative reformulation methods under strictly controlled conditions. It tests them with multiple LLMs at different scales, three retrieval paradigms (lexical keyword search, learned sparse search, dense neural search), and nine datasets. It publishes all prompts, configurations, and results via QueryGym, an open toolkit with a leaderboard.
1154.ww: By controlling variables systematically, the paper reveals which improvements are robust versus which are fragile. If a method only works with dense retrievers but not sparse ones, that's a finding. If larger LLMs don't help, that's worth knowing. Replication under uniform conditions grounds the field.
1154.po: Key finding: gains from reformulation are retriever-dependent—improvements on keyword search don't reliably transfer to neural retrievers. Larger LLMs don't uniformly help. QueryGym provides infrastructure for transparent comparison, so future work can build on verified successes rather than rediscovering failures.
